strengths: The paper investigates a relevant empirical question: whether captions originating in different languages contribute complementary visual concepts. The findings could inform annotation recruitment, training-data composition, and caption evaluation.

Equal-caption comparisons provide meaningful evidence of complementarity. In the human study, combining five English and five Japanese captions yields 9.90 objects per image, versus 9.13 for ten English captions and 8.97 for ten Japanese captions (Table 1).

The analysis includes human annotations, multiple captioning systems, and an English multimodel baseline. Grounded coverage also improves: Table 6 reports Visual Genome object recall increasing from 0.183 to 0.200 when replacing English-only captions with an equally sized English/French/Chinese mixture.

The explicit translation prompt and human translation audit, with a reported mean quality rating of 4.68/5, are useful methodological safeguards. The supplementary discussion acknowledges limitations of language as a cultural proxy and of the coverage metrics.
weaknesses: The evidence supports complementary caption content more convincingly than improved visual representations. Section 4 primarily measures adaptation to reference-caption distributions using SPICE. Multilingual training is competitive, but scores 0.244 on the mixed test set versus 0.246 for French-only training (Table 7). These results do not establish the stronger claim that multilingual training produces better visual understanding; an independent assessment of grounded correctness or transferable visual capability is missing.

A material reporting inconsistency weakens the training evidence: all 36 entries in Table 17, labeled as LLaVA-caption training, exactly reproduce the corresponding submatrix of Table 7, labeled as Vertex-caption training. This could be a reporting error, but the claimed independent replication cannot be credited from the manuscript as provided.

Most coverage measures reward additional or more dispersed text without establishing visual correctness. In Table 6, multilingual Vertex captions mention 4.31 objects but match only 3.84 annotated objects. The remaining 0.47 objects cannot systematically be classified as missing ground truth without separating genuine omissions from hallucinations and parsing or matching errors. Three selected examples in Table 16 do not establish the reported frequency of undocumented objects. Caption-length controls and systematic groundedness validation are also absent.

The cultural interpretation remains underdetermined. Model training distributions and unequal multilingual competence can produce language-dependent captions without demonstrating cultural perception. The human foreground/background interpretation relies on selected examples from 20 participants viewing 30 images, without a quantitative test of that distinction. The authors acknowledge these limitations, but stronger interpretations persist in the main narrative.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the precise Vertex model/version and decoding settings, GIT fine-tuning hyperparameters, and thresholds used to merge scene-graph concepts. Training results lack repeated-run uncertainty, while significance claims do not identify the statistical tests. Minor notation problems, such as describing a union as shared content and treating a quantity defined as error as higher-is-better, are correctable; the measurement and training-evidence concerns above determine the weak-reject recommendation.
